headline: A virus-scan reply that never says FOUND no longer stalls the scanner
summary: `b.mail.scan`'s ClamAV client read the threat name out of the daemon's reply with a pattern that could be made to take exponential time, and the reply is accepted up to 50 MiB. It reads the name in one pass now. The check that should have caught it was reading regex literals only and driving them with subjects of one repeated character, so it never saw the pattern reach its costly branch; widening it is what found this.

items.title: `b.mail.scan` reads a ClamAV reply in one pass
items.body:
The ClamAV INSTREAM client took the threat name out of `stream: <name> FOUND` with a lazy run between two whitespace quantifiers. A space matches both of them, so on a reply that never says FOUND the engine tries every way of dividing one run of spaces between the two before it can answer. Measured: 2,400 spaces cost 1.8 seconds, and 8,192 did not finish within five.

The daemon chooses that reply, and it is accepted up to `maxResponseBytes`, which is 50 MiB on the strict profile. So the size of that search belongs to whatever is on the other end of the socket, whether that is a compromised scanner, something in the path of an unencrypted connection to it, or a reply shaped by the file being scanned.

The name is read in one pass now, with the same result for every reply shape: a name never spans a line, the spaces around it may, and a reply carrying a clean line and an infected one is still read from the infected one, so an infection cannot be downgraded to clean.

Nothing to do on upgrade. Verdicts, threat names and audit records are unchanged.

items.title: Which text is a pattern is asked of the lexer
items.body:
The check found patterns by matching slashes across a line. Whether a `/` opens a pattern or divides two numbers or sits inside a string is a lexing question, and answering it with a search over the line got it wrong in both directions: 2,684 spans that are comment prose, URL paths inside strings and `/* */` openers were measured as patterns, while 5 real ones were missed.

The embedded WebAuthn attestation roots are where that showed. A base64 line of a certificate contains slashes, and the text between two of them parses as a pattern whose two `+` quantifiers measure superlinear once a probe reaches them, so the check was on course to report a certificate as a slow regular expression.

The framework already owns a lexer, and the comment rule already shares its classifier with the tool that sweeps comments. This now does the same, and reads the 613 patterns the library actually contains.

The lexer carries the `v` flag now, which it used to stop before, leaving the flag to be read as a name and the pattern rebuilt without it. What that flag enables is character classes that nest, which this reader does not parse, so a pattern using it is refused with that reason rather than measured under a shape that might not be the one that runs. The framework has no such pattern today.

items.title: Composed patterns are measured for linear time
items.body:
The linear-time check extracts regex literals from the source. A pattern built with `new RegExp("...")`, or through a helper that wraps one, is not a literal, so 34 of them were measured by nothing. That included every entry in the table `b.guardSql` matches statements against, which is the one place in the framework a regex is pointed at hostile SQL by design.

Both shapes are reconstructed and measured now: a direct `new RegExp` on a string, and a one-argument helper that wraps `new RegExp` with fixed flags. A pattern assembled from a variable or a `join()` cannot be rebuilt without running the file and is still left to the module's own tests.

All 34 measure linear. Four of them are refused by `b.guardRegex.assertSafe`, which is the framework's own conservative screen; they now carry a measurement rather than an assertion.

items.title: A pattern is driven past its opening literal
items.body:
Subjects were built from one character repeated. A pattern that opens with a literal fails at that token on such a subject and never reaches what follows it, so a costly body behind `\bCOPY\b` was measured on nothing and read as fast. The prefix a pattern insists on is now read off it verbatim, punctuation included, and seeded into subjects of its own. Where a pattern requires several literals in order, the runs joined in order are seeded too, because a subject carrying one of them stops at the next. The filler is drawn from the characters the pattern itself names, since `a` and a space do not enter a body that wants `x`, and each subject is tried with a trailing character the pattern cannot accept, because a pattern only backtracks on its way to failing.

That is what found the ClamAV defect above. Reading the prefix as words joined by spaces was not enough on its own: `stream:` keeps its colon only when the prefix is taken verbatim.

items.title: An exemption marker is checked wherever it is written
items.body:
A marker that exempts a line from a rule was validated in `lib/` and `test/` only. Everywhere else it could name whatever it liked. Five markers had been sitting outside that scope, all spelling a class renamed in an earlier pass specifically so that every use would be re-examined; the rename reached the markers the check could see and left these. None of them exempted anything, since the rule they named reads the framework's own source and not those files, so they are removed.

The check now reads scripts and the example apps too, skipping installed dependencies and build output. The example app runs a gate of its own with its own classes, so a marker under `examples/` is answered against that registry rather than the framework's; a name in neither is still reported.

items.title: A rule's advertised exemption is the one it honors
items.body:
Each rule heads itself with the marker that exempts a site, which is where a reader goes when the build stops on them. Ten named a class that had been renamed, so following one produced a marker the repository then refuses. Two more named a class that is registered while the rule never consults it, so the marker was accepted, did nothing, and said nothing: the build failed again with the message the contributor had just tried to answer.

The ten now name the class they filter on. The two rules take no marker at all, which they now say, and their classes are retired so writing one is refused rather than ignored. Eight more rules that never took a marker say so on the line, which keeps their name and keeps the claim checkable.

A new check holds all of it, and asks the question per rule rather than across the file: a rule may not advertise a retired class, nor a registered class it does not consult, nor a class that is neither registered nor consulted anywhere, since that last one names an exemption no contributor can spend.
